# B4. Identification of X {#oecd-leisure}

As for Argentina ([A3](arg-leisure.qmd)), the paper takes the taste for leisure $X$ common to the income groups and
pins its level by each country's average workweek; the alternative identifies one $X_i$ per group from the observed
relative hours. In every country the two calibrations share the discount factor, the political weight of the old,
the tax rate, savings and aggregate hours. They also share every counterfactual that changes neither the
productivities nor the taste for leisure: the design, ageing and France's voting patterns. The tables and the figure
show only what differs.

## The calibration {#oecd-leisure-calibration}

Two rows of the paper's calibration table differ, the taste for leisure and the productivity spread. Under the
vector $X_i$ the taste for leisure rises with income in all three countries: observed hours rise less with income
than the common $X$ predicts, the high group working fewer hours than predicted. To reproduce the same relative
incomes with those hours, the productivity spread widens.

{{< include _generated/exhibits/OECD_LeisureCalibration.qmd >}}

Group by group, the vector $X_i$ are a fraction of the common $X$, and their level carries no information of its own.
Under the common $X$ the level is the unit of hours: it is set so that the model's average workweek is the observed
one, relative to the U.S. for the UK and France, and the productivities scale with it. Under the vector $X_i$ the
relative hours fix only the ratios of the $X_i$, and the unit is a normalization. That is why the level differs so
much between the two while every aggregate is the same.

{{< include _generated/exhibits/OECD_LeisureGroups.qmd >}}

## The counterfactuals that differ {#oecd-leisure-rows}

France's income distribution is imposed through the productivities and its leisure preferences through the taste
for leisure, so these are the rows the treatment of leisure moves, with the row that imposes all of France's
characteristics at once. On the U.S. the vector $X_i$ strengthens the
effect of France's income distribution at every IES and makes that of its leisure preferences on hours a little
smaller. On the UK the effect of France's income distribution on the tax rate changes sign. The vector $X_i$ read part
of the observed income dispersion off relative hours, which are much flatter in the UK than in France, so at the UK's
income cuts France's productivity spread falls below the UK's, where under the common $X$ it lies above.

::: {.oa-explorer .column-page}
{{< include _generated/exhibits/OECD_LeisureRows-head.qmd >}}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {counterfactuals, control, RHO, GIVEN_OUTCOMES} from "./assets/oa.js"
oecd = FileAttachment("_generated/data/OECD_Counterfactuals.csv").csv({typed: true})
viewof b4Host = control("radio", [["U.S.", "US"], ["UK", "UK"]], {key: "host", label: "Host", value: "US"})
viewof b4Out = control("radio", GIVEN_OUTCOMES, {key: "outcome", label: "Outcome", value: "tau"})
counterfactuals(oecd.filter(d => d.source === "main" && d.effect === "full" && d.host === b4Host),
  {rows: [{label: "French income distr.", scenario: "income"}, {label: "French leisure", scenario: "leisure"},
          {label: "All French characteristics", scenario: "frall"}],
   series: RHO, outcome: b4Out, width,
   facets: [{label: "Common X, the paper's", filter: d => d.calibration === "commonX"},
            {label: "Vector Xᵢ", filter: d => d.calibration === "vectorX"}]})
```
